tier_reason: timings.csv in the third-party kadyb/vector-benchmark repo has every quoted median (e.g. distance 0.11 GeometryOps vs 0.9 GeoPandas vs 5.37 R geos; intersects 0.04 vs 0.12 vs 0.08), and the suite owner (kadyb) re-ran all packages himself ('update benchmark results', 2025-09-24), so this is an independent measurement. It is not A: the scripts are public and the CPU (Ryzen 9 5900X) is stated, but no Julia/R/Python versions are given and the package versions are only partly pinned.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Median seconds in timings.csv, GeometryOps.jl vs GEOS-backed packages, on tasks where GeometryOps runs its own pure-Julia code: distance 0.11 vs 0.9 (GeoPandas) and 5.37 (R geos); intersects 0.04 vs 0.12 (GeoPandas) and 0.08 (R geos, prepared geometry); sample 0.04 vs 0.9 (GeoPandas). Derived ratios (derived from page data): distance about 8x vs GeoPandas and about 49x vs R geos; intersects 3x vs GeoPandas and 2x vs R geos; sample about 22x vs GeoPandas. The other tasks are not GeometryOps-vs-GEOS comparisons: buffer is 5.75 vs 4.07 (GeoPandas) and 5.65 (R geos), but the GeometryOps buffer script calls GEOS itself through LibGEOS (GO.GEOS backend), so it is GEOS vs GEOS; transform 0.08 vs 0.23 (GeoPandas) runs PROJ through Proj.jl on both sides, and R sf-project also takes 0.08; load 0.36 vs 0.45 (GeoPandas) and write 1.38 vs 1.28 are GDAL file I/O, and terra loads faster (0.33).
corrections.workload: kadyb/vector-benchmark: a synthetic set of 500,000 planar points plus one polygon. The distance task uses only the first 5,000 points (a 5,000 x 5,000 pairwise distance matrix). intersects tests all 500,000 points against the polygon. The other tasks are buffer, sampling points in the polygon, CRS transform, and GeoPackage load/write. Each value is the median seconds per task. Julia is timed with Chairmarks for 15 s (60 s for buffer) after warm-up; R uses system.time and Python uses timeit, 10 runs each.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Interpreted/JIT packages (Julia, Python, R); no Julia, R or Python version stated. geometryops/Project.toml sets compat GeometryOps = 0.1.26; pixi.toml pins geopandas >=1.1.1,<2, pandas >=2.3.2, numpy >=2.3.2 and pyogrio >=0.11.1,<0.12; R package versions are not pinned.
corrections.caveats: Only distance, intersects and sample compare GeometryOps' own pure-Julia code against GEOS. In buffer, GeometryOps calls GEOS itself via LibGEOS. Transform is PROJ on both sides, and load/write are GDAL I/O, so none of those are GEOS comparisons. GEOS is reached through wrappers (GeoPandas/Shapely, R 'geos'), so per-call marshalling overhead is part of the baseline. The R geos distance time (5.37 s) comes from an sapply loop over geos_distance, one row at a time. The script's commented-out alternatives (a matrix loop and a fully vectorised call) are noted at about 11 s, so the R wrapper itself, not just the loop style, looks like the bottleneck. Julia is timed after JIT warm-up with Chairmarks, while R/Python take the median of 10 cold-start-inclusive runs. Each package's scripts were written by that package's developers: the Julia side by GeometryOps lead asinghvi17 (PR #12, 2024) and JuliaGeo's evetion (PRs #15-#17, 2025), and the GeoPandas side updated by GeoPandas maintainer martinfleis (PR #18). The suite owner kadyb re-ran everything on one machine. Suite repo: 23 stars, MIT. Its detailed report is on github.io and was not reachable. GeometryOps' README points at this suite and says 'More benchmarks coming soon', and the package warns it is under heavy development. Julia is outside the 'usable from C++' scope.

notes: Numbers verified against timings.csv; benchmark scripts read. Main fix: buffer (GEOS via LibGEOS), transform (PROJ vs PROJ) and load/write (GDAL) are not GeometryOps-vs-GEOS wins or losses, and the distance task uses 5,000 points rather than 500,000. Metadata matches: MIT, 84 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-09-20.

tier_reason: The README's 'Benchmark (preliminary)' block shows Create 1165 vs 25522 us, Update 851 vs 3824 us and IterateAllCells 124 vs 698 us against Octomap. The matching Google Benchmark code is public (bonxai_core/benchmark/benchmark_bonxai.cpp and benchmark_octomap.cpp), but no compiler, flags, CPU or dataset is given for the published numbers, so this is first-party C.

corrections.workload: Google Benchmark in bonxai_core/benchmark (benchmark_bonxai.cpp vs benchmark_octomap.cpp) on two PCD point clouds from data/: table_scene_mug_rgb.pcd at 0.01 voxel size and room_scan.pcd at 0.05. Create inserts every point into a new grid, Update re-sets the same cells in a filled grid, and IterateAllCells visits every leaf. The README does not say which dataset its numbers come from.
corrections.caveats: The README labels the numbers 'preliminary' and says to take them with a grain of salt. It gives no compiler, flags, CPU or dataset; the default CMake build type is RelWithDebInfo. The two sides do not do the same work per point: Bonxai writes a uint32 value with accessor.setValue, while Octomap runs OcTree::updateNode(endpoint, true), a probabilistic log-odds occupancy update. That favors Bonxai in Create and Update. A fairer full-mapping comparison, bonxai_map/benchmark/benchmark_kitti.cpp (probabilistic map with ray casting vs Octomap on KITTI, prints a speed-up), exists, but no results from it are published. The README also says the project is built mostly for fun and education and is under development, and that very sparse clouds can use 20-40% more memory than Octomap. The Octomap baseline is a robotics-mapping incumbent rather than Boost.Geometry/CGAL/GEOS, so the category fit is borderline.

notes: Numbers match the README. I found and read the benchmark source the searcher could not locate. Main finding: Octomap does a probabilistic occupancy update per point while Bonxai only stores a value, so the comparison is not like-for-like. Metadata matches: MPL-2.0, 879 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-09-28.

tier_reason: doc/voronoi_benchmark.htm has the quoted tables, and the benchmark code is public (benchmark/voronoi_benchmark_points.cpp, benchmark/voronoi_benchmark_segments.cpp). It names the compiler (GCC 4.7.3) and CPU, but the optimization flags and b2 build variant are not stated and Jamfile.v2 sets none, so it is not A. The library author ran it, so first-party C.

corrections.caveats: Mixed result: only segment input wins (about 1.3x to 1.56x vs CGAL's Segment_Delaunay_graph_2, derived from page data). For points, CGAL's Delaunay_triangulation_2 (Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions kernel) is about 3.8x faster at 1M points (derived from page data). Voronoi and Delaunay are different outputs; the page notes the Voronoi diagram carries more information. In the segments test, the time for generating segments and removing intersections is measured in a separate pass and subtracted, and timing is CPU time (user+system) from boost::timer::cpu_timer. benchmark/Jamfile.v2 hard-codes the author's local library paths and sets no optimization flags. b2's default variant is debug unless variant=release is passed, and the page does not say which was used. This is a first-party benchmark by the library author with an old setup (GCC 4.7.3, Boost 1.54, CGAL 4.3-beta1, Ubuntu 13.04). The page was last edited 2013-10-06 ('rerunning benchmarks'), so its CPU label 'Intel i5-7600 2.8 GHz' predates that CPU's 2017 release and is likely a typo; reported as printed. A WebSearch snippet of the boost.org copy summarised the result as complete dominance over the CGAL Delaunay graph, which the points table does not support. boost.org was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the repo copy was read. doc/analysis.htm separately says the 2010 divide-and-conquer Booleans are 'roughly as fast as GPC at small scales, while algorithmically faster at large scales', with no GPC numbers.

notes: All table values were checked against the repo copy of voronoi_benchmark.htm and the benchmark sources were read. Metadata matches: BSL-1.0 in the file headers, 70 stars, not archived, last commit 2025-05-02, so stale. The 1.56x segment win stands; the points loss is documented.
